newsitem.title: CHINA: China forex reserves not too high-Business Weekly.
newsitem.headline: China forex reserves not too high-Business Weekly.

text.p: China's foreign exchange reserves, which hit $110 billion last month, are not too high in view of the needs of development, debt repayment and remittances by foreign investors, the Business Weekly said on Sunday.
It quoted an official of the State Administration of Foreign Exchange as saying that current levels were appropriate considering the nation's foreign exchange requirements.
Reserves sufficient to cover three months' worth of imports -- about $60 billion -- were not enough, the newspaper quoted the official as saying.
"In fact, the economic development in China requires a relatively high reserve," he said.
China announced it had reserves of $110 billion at the end of last month. Reserves reached $105 billion at the end of last year, up $31.5 billion from the beginning of 1996.
The official, who was not identified by name, said China had foreign debt of over $116 billion and the repayment period was around its peak.

The newspaper, published by the official China Daily, quoted the official as saying that total foreign investment in the country had reached about $170 billion and that meant foreign investors would remit about $20 billion a year outside the country.
But the official said that Beijing did not believe that the more reserves it had the better.
He said that the high levels had come at a price, adding that some funds were left idle. He noted that interest paid on debt was higher than interest earned on the nation's reserves.
But he said the rising reserves enhanced the nation's payment ability and credit, and that meant lower borrowing costs.
He also said the nation did not want to see a sharp appreciation of the local currency, the yuan, as that would hurt exporters.
It also did not want to see a major expansion of credit to stimulate growth and use some of the foreign reserves.
China has been trying to hold the line on credit expansion in order to keep tight control over inflation.
